segments.t: Arriving at the Seminci film festival red carpet in Valladolid, Paquita hands Macarena over to festival coordinator Sofi and pretends she is driving back to Madrid for the wedding drinks. Before leaving, Paquita calls out across the crowd to let Macarena know she understands — telling her that whatever dress she wears, she will always look gorgeous. Listen to the Spanish first.
Hola, Sofi, ¿qué tal? Oye, cuídamela.
Prometido.
He pensado que mejor me vuelvo a Madrid.
¿Por qué?
Porque estoy cansada. ¿Qué hago yo aquí vestida así?
Si me doy prisa, quizá llego a las copas de la boda.
Sí, pero ¿estás bien?
Sí, de verdad, todo bien. Tú no te preocupes.
Gracias por traerme.
¡Maca!
¿Qué?
Que tú estás guapísima siempre.
Da igual el vestido que te pongas, estarás guapísima siempre.
Gracias, Paquita.
Gracias a ti. Corre, venga.
Let's walk through their farewell on the red carpet.
Hola, Sofi, ¿qué tal? Oye, cuídamela.
'Hello, Sofi, how are things? Hey, take good care of her for me.' Look how much affection fits into that final four-syllable word: look after, plus for me, plus feminine her for Macarena.
Prometido.
'Promised.' Using the masculine singular past form of promise all by itself is a crisp, reusable one-word reply meaning I promise or consider it done.
He pensado que mejor me vuelvo a Madrid.
'I've decided I'd better head back to Madrid.' Literally I have thought that better I return myself to Madrid, adding myself to return for the casual feel of heading back.
¿Por qué?
'Why?' Two short words ask why: the word for followed by accented what.
Porque estoy cansada. ¿Qué hago yo aquí vestida así?
'Because I'm tired. What am I doing here dressed like this?' Notice how two-word why is answered immediately by one-word unaccented because! Both tired and dressed end in feminine a for Paquita.
Si me doy prisa, quizá llego a las copas de la boda.

'If I hurry, maybe I'll make the wedding drinks.' Earlier having haste meant being in a hurry; giving yourself haste means hurrying up. Plural glasses also means the late-night drinks party at a Spanish wedding.
Sí, pero ¿estás bien?
'Yes, but are you alright?' Pairing are you with the word for well checks how someone is feeling right now, rather than describing permanent character.
Sí, de verdad, todo bien. Tú no te preocupes.
'Yes, honestly, everything's fine. Don't you worry.' Putting casual you right at the front of don't worry gently shifts Macarena's focus back onto her own big night.
Gracias por traerme.
'Thank you for bringing me.' After thanks for, Spanish uses the basic to-form with me attached, literally thanks for to bring me, rather than an ing-form.
¡Maca!
'Maca!' Calling out Macarena's short nickname across the crowd stops her just before she enters theatre.
¿Qué?
'What?' Turning back toward Paquita, Macarena answers with the single accented question word for what.
Que tú estás guapísima siempre.
'You always look gorgeous.' Starting a shouted sentence with the linking word for that is classic spoken Spanish, as if continuing I'm telling you that you always look gorgeous.
Da igual el vestido que te pongas, estarás guapísima siempre.
'Never mind which dress you put on, you'll always look gorgeous.' Answering Macarena's metaphor at last, Paquita pairs the phrase for never mind with future-tense you will look.
Gracias, Paquita.
'Thank you, Paquita.' Hearing that Paquita knows and forgives her, Macarena answers with the plural word for thanks followed by Paquita's name.
Gracias a ti. Corre, venga.
'Thank you. Go on, run along.' Returning thanks with thanks to you stresses you in reply, and literally run sends Macarena warmly down the carpet. Now let's listen to the whole scene again.
Hola, Sofi, ¿qué tal? Oye, cuídamela.
Prometido.
He pensado que mejor me vuelvo a Madrid.
¿Por qué?
Porque estoy cansada. ¿Qué hago yo aquí vestida así?
Si me doy prisa, quizá llego a las copas de la boda.
Sí, pero ¿estás bien?
Sí, de verdad, todo bien. Tú no te preocupes.
Gracias por traerme.
¡Maca!
¿Qué?
Que tú estás guapísima siempre.
Da igual el vestido que te pongas, estarás guapísima siempre.
Gracias, Paquita.
Gracias a ti. Corre, venga.
You heard how 'cuídamela' packs 'look after her for me' into one word, 'darse prisa' for hurrying, and Paquita's parting blessing 'estarás guapísima siempre'. Congratulations on completing Episode 1!
¡Adiós!
